comments.author: William Briere
comments.text: I do not agree with the decisions based on poll numbers, as they can be highly misleading. Discussions about Alberta's future should be left to Albertans, especially given the history of federal policies that have negatively impacted the province. Furthermore, I believe voting rights should be tied to employment status; voting should belong to the working people who put food on the table, particularly those working outside major cities. It is clear that urban centers tend to lean Liberal, which skews political outcomes. While I agree that Alberta should remain a part of Canada, Ottawa must keep its hands off Alberta's natural resources and allow the province to make its own decisions. It is exhausting to see Western Canada contribute billions of dollars annually to Ottawa, essentially subsidizing a better standard of living for the East.

comments.author: susannet6h
comments.text:
I'd love to see that math. To be clear, Alberta doesn't send anything to the feds. Canadian citizens and corporations pay tax to the federal government, then the government distributes that money to make sure that all Canadian citizens can access adequate government services. Albertan residents and corporations pay more in tax than Canadians elsewhere because they're making more. But they pay the same percentage. If Alberta wants more money, it could always limit corporate profits. But the real question is when did Albertans become so selfish? What do we gain from refusing to share the wealth? Money is tight--which is why we should start demanding that companies pay us what we're truly worth. Why would we begrudge a Newfie fisherman healthcare, but subsidize an American-owned refinery? 

Also, Alberta isn't governed by an especially wise and fiscally responsible party. We just happen to sit on a lot of oil. It's much easier to be in the black with a strong income. That's luck, not merit or good management. If oil prices fall, we'll be in deficit territory instantly.

comments.text: About the "federal paramountcy" discussion -- Yes, the federal bankruptcy law can "discharge debts" in bankruptcy ... But since the vehicle-licensing laws are all solely provincial, Alberta can permanently bar the driver from obtaining a driver's licence or vehicle permits, due to the driver history; having been driving while uninsured; and having declared bankruptcy to avoid paying a legal debt owed to the provincial government. Sure, the person no longer has to pay the debt, but Alberta would be in its rights to permanently bar the driver from driving in Alberta.

It is eventually up to the Supreme Court to resolve, though in my opinion, a province should check 1st if their law could be in conflict with a federal one as this issue suggests.

If it is insufficient then the province covers the rest in this case where bankruptcy absolves the person from further debt recovery.

The principle is the government that initially creates the law has precedence at least until a court either strikes down the law or determines the conflict for the other government.

Also governments should be able to be sued by insurance firms if the government does not enforce license requirements like insurance and restrictions on using the vehicle.

comments.text:
I often wonder what all the fuss is about. I have lived and worked across this great country of ours landing here in Alberta 30 years ago. Alberta has been good to me with steady work, good pay and a pension to finish up with.

Honestly, Alberta enjoys the best economy in Canada (most of the time...when oil prices are up. Not so good when down). No provincial sales tax and other Alberta only perks. Although it can get bitingly cold in the winter, generally a good climate. What is there to complain about? 

On the other hand, I note that the study discussed in the adjoining article doesn't take into account the exodus of population if separation becomes likely. This happened in both Quebec referendi even though the outcome of both was a positive - stay in Canada. Businesses, corporations and people left the province in large numbers. Calgary and Edmonton both received a significant number of corporate head offices relocating. The Quebec economy really hasn't recovered the status it had before the votes and its been over 45 years since the latest one. 

If even 10% of Alberta's current population decide they no longer want to reside in a separate country, the effect on house prices and other factors will be devastating to the average household. Even more may decide to leave. Remember that perhaps as mauch as 50% of the current population were not born in Alberta.
